cls: Centrally acting skeletal muscle relaxant (aryl glyceryl ether; ATC M03BX06)
pharm: An older centrally acting skeletal muscle relaxant (an aryl glyceryl ether related to guaifenesin and methocarbamol) that depresses polysynaptic spinal reflexes to relieve muscle spasm. Largely obsolete and superseded by safer agents; not FDA-approved.

summary: Mephenesin is an old centrally acting skeletal muscle relaxant (an aryl glyceryl ether, structurally related to guaifenesin and methocarbamol, and the chemical forerunner of meprobamate). It relieves painful muscle spasm by depressing polysynaptic spinal reflexes and interneuronal transmission, without acting at the neuromuscular junction. It is largely obsolete: it has a short duration of action and a low therapeutic index with prominent CNS and respiratory depression, and the historical intravenous formulation was abandoned because it caused hemolysis, hemoglobinuria, and thrombophlebitis. It is NOT FDA-approved and is no longer marketed in North America (the French OTC product Decontractyl was discontinued in 2019). Dosing figures vary between drug-information sources and should be confirmed against the local label; alcohol and other CNS depressants must be avoided. NOTE: This record is based on EMA/SmPC-style, BNF/Martindale, and secondary drug-information references because mephenesin is not FDA-approved; doses and pharmacokinetic figures are source-dependent and should be verified locally.

Topical combination preparations are used for local musculoskeletal pain (region-specific)

moa: Mephenesin acts centrally, predominantly within the spinal cord, depressing polysynaptic (interneuronal/internuncial) reflex transmission while having relatively little effect on the monosynaptic stretch reflex. By reducing transmission through spinal interneuron pathways it decreases excessive muscle tone and spasm. It does not act at the neuromuscular junction or directly on skeletal muscle. Its action is greater on the spinal cord than on the brain; proposed secondary effects on GABAergic/glutamatergic transmission are reported in secondary sources but are less well established.

absolute: Known hypersensitivity to mephenesin or any formulation component
relative: Concurrent use of CNS depressants or alcohol
monitor: Level of sedation and respiratory status

preg: There are insufficient data on use in pregnancy; no authoritative pregnancy category is available. Secondary sources advise caution and to avoid use unless clearly necessary.
lact: Data on excretion in breast milk are lacking; avoid use during breastfeeding unless clearly necessary.
renal: Mephenesin is excreted predominantly by the kidneys (partly unchanged). No validated dose-adjustment scheme is available; use caution and avoid in significant renal impairment.
hepatic: Mephenesin is metabolized in the liver. No validated dose-adjustment scheme is available; use caution and avoid in significant hepatic impairment.

major: Alcohol - additive CNS and respiratory depression (potentially dangerous)
Other CNS depressants (benzodiazepines, opioids, barbiturates, sedatives) - additive sedation and respiratory depression
moderate: Other skeletal muscle relaxants - additive weakness and excessive muscle relaxation
minor: Enzyme inducers (e.g., phenobarbital, rifampicin) may reduce plasma levels (secondary-source claim)

missed: If you miss a dose, take it when you remember unless it is almost time for the next dose, in which case skip the missed dose. Do not take a double dose to make up for a missed one.
overdose: Overdose produces exaggerated CNS and respiratory depression, with risk markedly increased by concurrent alcohol or other depressants. There is no specific antidote; management is supportive, with attention to airway, breathing (ventilatory support if needed), and circulation.
